provenance.accuracy: Orbit solutions from video meteor observations. The shape and tilt of each orbit are measured; its semi-major axis is the weakest element. Orbit elements are as listed (observed); the position along each orbit is illustrative.
provenance.notes: Global Meteor Network trajectory summary, monthly files 202507, 202508, IAU shower 7: 32234 records, 6619 unbound or incomplete records dropped, 25588 bound orbits in the file, 25588 orbits drawn (all orbits). Fetched 2026-10-16T09:20:16.344Z. Licence CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/), credit the Global Meteor Network. Each orbit's shape and orientation come from its record, but the records give no position along the orbit: that position is an even spread of mean anomaly at the reference time, a drawing choice (illustrative), advanced by unperturbed two-body motion about the centre. A stated share of the dots is placed near the reference body's position along the orbit: a model, not a measurement. No orbit is added.

object.label: Perseids stream
object.description: 25588 measured meteoroid orbits of the Perseids, each drawn as one dot (Global Meteor Network trajectory summary, monthly files 202507, 202508). The orbits' shapes and tilts are measured; where each dot sits along its orbit is illustrative, and the clump near 109P/Swift-Tuttle is a model. One item stands for the whole stream; its focus point is the centroid of the dots.
knownLimitations: Orbit set shown: all orbits (25588 bound orbits). This file carries no per-orbit quality columns, so it cannot be cut to a reliable set. Of 25588 bound orbits, 23335 pass the published quality cut (convergence angle Qc at least 15 deg and Vgeo sigma at most 10% of Vgeo) and 2253 fail it. The cut is the published rule: "requiring a minimum convergence angle of 15 degrees between cameras, ensuring an estimated velocity error of no more than 10% of the nominal value" (the 2025 HDBSCAN paper words it: "a minimum convergence angle of 15° between camera detections to ensure reliable triangulation, ... a velocity error not exceeding 10% of the nominal value"); both apply it to the CAMS v3.0 database; they also drop hyperbolic orbits, which the data file already does (Peña-Asensio and Sánchez-Lozano 2024, Statistical Equivalence of Metrics for Meteor Dynamical Association, Advances in Space Research, doi 10.1016/j.asr.2024.05.005 (arXiv 2405.03308); and arXiv 2507.01501, Meteoroid stream identification with HDBSCAN, https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.03308), mapped to GMN's own columns: Qc is GMN's own maximum convergence angle between stations (column Qc, deg) and the Vgeo sigma is the uncertainty column beside Vgeo (km/s), so the reliable set is Qc at least the angle and sigma at most the fraction of Vgeo. GMN has no double-entry flag.
The position of each dot along its orbit is illustrative: the records give each orbit's shape and tilt, not where the meteoroid is. The dots are spread evenly round their orbits.

The clump near 109P/Swift-Tuttle is a model: 30% of the dots are placed within ±20° of 109P/Swift-Tuttle's orbital phase (illustrative defaults: not a published fit. 20 degrees of mean anomaly either side is about 15 years of the 133-year orbit. Young dust is known to crowd near the parent (the early-1990s Perseid outbursts followed the comet's 1992 return), but no published fraction or width is claimed.) The orbits differ in size, so the clump shows as a band at 109P/Swift-Tuttle's phase, not a blob on 109P/Swift-Tuttle.
Parts of the stream that miss Earth are not shown: the database holds only meteoroids that reached Earth.
The semi-major axis of a measured orbit is poorly determined (the speed error dominates it), so the sizes of the orbits are less certain than their shape and tilt.

panels.title: A river of comet dust
body: Each dot follows the real path of a grain of comet dust. Cameras on Earth measured that path when the grain burned up as a shooting star.
Together, more than 25,000 of them trace a wide ribbon along the orbit of comet Swift–Tuttle.
details: The dots are about 25,600 Perseid orbits measured by the Global Meteor Network's cameras in July and August 2025. Together they trace a wide ribbon of dust along the orbit of comet Swift–Tuttle.

The orbits are measured. Where each dot sits along its orbit is not: those places are illustrative, chosen to show the ribbon's shape, so the pattern of dots along the ribbon says nothing about where the dust really is.
More than 25,000: 25,588 bound orbits are drawn.

The demo shows the year from 21 September 2019 to 20 September 2020. The orbits were measured in 2025 and are drawn as they are, a measured shape with illustrative places along it, in that earlier year; this moment, 1 November 2019, is six weeks into it.
sources: Global Meteor Network, monthly trajectory summaries, Jul and Aug 2025, IAU shower 7 (PER); Vida et al. 2021, MNRAS 506(4); Vida et al. 2020, MNRAS 491(2); CC BY 4.0; globalmeteornetwork.org/data (accessed 2026-10-16)
Astraeus docs/ASTRONOMY_VALIDATION.md, GMN section (O-011 / T-056): 25,588 bound orbits drawn; the dots' places along their orbits are illustrative

panels.title: Earth meets the dust
body: Earth passes through this ribbon every year, from mid-July to late August.
The dust burns up in our sky as shooting stars: up to about 100 an hour on the best night, under a perfectly dark sky.
They all seem to fly out of the constellation Perseus, which gives the shower its name.
details: Once a year Earth passes through the ribbon. The Perseids are active from mid-July to late August (17 July to 24 August) and peak on the night of 12–13 August, at about 100 meteors an hour at best (a zenithal hourly rate, ZHR, of 100: the rate one observer would see under a perfectly dark sky with the radiant overhead). They seem to come from a point in the constellation Perseus.
In 2020, the year this scene shows, the International Meteor Organization gave the activity as 17 July to 24 August and the peak as 12 August between 13:00 and 16:00 UT.

The peak in this scene is 12 August 2020 at 15:41:56 UTC: the moment the Sun reaches solar longitude 140.1° (J2000), the IAU Meteor Data Center's peak, found on the engine's ephemeris; it falls inside the International Meteor Organization's 13:00 to 16:00 UT.

In the 2025 measured orbits, the stream passes closest to Earth about 2.2 hours before the official peak, and its radiant lies 0.04° from the IAU's. Those figures were measured against the August 2027 peak; against the 12 August 2020 peak this scene shows, the closest pass is about 2.3 hours before the peak (1.3 hours in the reliable set) and the radiant lies 0.06° from the IAU's.
sources: IAU Meteor Data Center, Perseids (PER, 7): peak solar longitude 140.1°, radiant RA 47.9°, Dec +57.9° (J2000); ta3.sk (accessed 2026-10-13)

panels.title: Where the dust comes from
body: All this dust comes from comet Swift–Tuttle, a huge lump of ice and rock.
Each time it swings close to the Sun it sheds a little more dust, then sails far out beyond Neptune.
It won't be back near the Sun until 2126.
details: The dust comes from comet Swift–Tuttle, whose nucleus is about 26 km across. It takes about 133 years to orbit the Sun, last passed closest to it in December 1992, and is next due in 2126.
At the far end of its orbit the comet is about 51 AU from the Sun (51 times Earth's distance from the Sun), well beyond Neptune.
2126 is the 1992 closest pass plus one orbital period: a two-body figure, not a perturbed prediction.

In this scene, in 2019 and 2020, the comet is about 39 AU from the Sun. Its drawn place was compared with JPL Horizons at six dates across the year: within about 7.6 million km, 0.13% of its distance from the Sun.
sources: NASA/JPL Small-Body Database, 109P/Swift-Tuttle, solution SB405-CPV-2: diameter 26 km (Lamy et al. 2004, Comets II); period 48,681.19 d (about 133.3 years); time of perihelion JD 2448968.4998 TDB (1992 Dec 11); aphelion 51.22 au; https://ssd-api.jpl.nasa.gov/sbdb.api?sstr=109P&full-prec=1&phys-par=1 (accessed 2026-10-15)
Next perihelion: the 1992 perihelion plus one period, JD about 2497650, early 2126 (a two-body figure, not a perturbed prediction)

object.label: Geminids stream
object.description: 51115 measured meteoroid orbits of the Geminids, each drawn as one dot (Global Meteor Network trajectory summary, monthly files 202412, 202512). The orbits' shapes and tilts are measured; where each dot sits along its orbit is illustrative, and the clump near 3200 Phaethon is a model. One item stands for the whole stream; its focus point is the centroid of the dots.
knownLimitations: Orbit set shown: all orbits (51115 bound orbits). This file carries no per-orbit quality columns, so it cannot be cut to a reliable set. Of 51115 bound orbits, 46828 pass the published quality cut (convergence angle Qc at least 15 deg and Vgeo sigma at most 10% of Vgeo) and 4287 fail it. The cut is the published rule: "requiring a minimum convergence angle of 15 degrees between cameras, ensuring an estimated velocity error of no more than 10% of the nominal value" (the 2025 HDBSCAN paper words it: "a minimum convergence angle of 15° between camera detections to ensure reliable triangulation, ... a velocity error not exceeding 10% of the nominal value"); both apply it to the CAMS v3.0 database; they also drop hyperbolic orbits, which the data file already does (Peña-Asensio and Sánchez-Lozano 2024, Statistical Equivalence of Metrics for Meteor Dynamical Association, Advances in Space Research, doi 10.1016/j.asr.2024.05.005 (arXiv 2405.03308); and arXiv 2507.01501, Meteoroid stream identification with HDBSCAN, https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.03308), mapped to GMN's own columns: Qc is GMN's own maximum convergence angle between stations (column Qc, deg) and the Vgeo sigma is the uncertainty column beside Vgeo (km/s), so the reliable set is Qc at least the angle and sigma at most the fraction of Vgeo. GMN has no double-entry flag.
The position of each dot along its orbit is illustrative: the records give each orbit's shape and tilt, not where the meteoroid is. The dots are spread evenly round their orbits.

The clump near 3200 Phaethon is a model: 0% of the dots are placed within ±20° of 3200 Phaethon's orbital phase (illustrative defaults: no clump is drawn. The Geminid stream is old and broad, and no published fraction or width of dust near Phaethon is claimed; every dot is a measured orbit spread uniformly in mean anomaly.) The orbits differ in size, so the clump shows as a band at 3200 Phaethon's phase, not a blob on 3200 Phaethon.
Parts of the stream that miss Earth are not shown: the database holds only meteoroids that reached Earth.
The semi-major axis of a measured orbit is poorly determined (the speed error dominates it), so the sizes of the orbits are less certain than their shape and tilt.

panels.title: A rock that behaves like a comet
body: Most meteor showers are dust shed by comets, icy balls that crumble as they pass the Sun. The Geminids come from Phaethon instead, a lump of rock only a few kilometres wide.

Every 17 months it swings closer to the Sun than Mercury ever gets; its last close pass was in early July 2019. The heat may crack its surface and shed grit, but exactly how it made so much dust is still a puzzle.
details: Phaethon's closest passes of the Sun (perihelion) either side of this year, from JPL Horizons (solution JPL#1019): JD 2458667.4947 TDB, 2 July 2019 at about 23:51 UTC, and JD 2459191.1021 TDB, 7 December 2020 at about 14:26 UTC, every 523.7 days (about 17 months). Neither falls inside the year the demo shows (21 September 2019 to 20 September 2020), so this panel opens on 1 November 2019, six weeks in and before the shower begins, when Phaethon is about 1.9 AU from the Sun on its way out.

The scene moves Phaethon by unperturbed two-body motion from published elements. Across this year its drawn place is within about 366,000 km of JPL Horizons (compared at six dates); near the Sun it can be off by up to about 935,000 km (see the asteroid's position accuracy).
At perihelion Phaethon is about 0.140 AU from the Sun, roughly 21 million km. Mercury's closest distance to the Sun is 46.0 million km.

Size: JPL gives an effective diameter of 6.25 km (Taylor et al. 2019, from radar); NASA's Geminids page gives 5.1 km. Phaethon was discovered on 11 October 1983 by the Infrared Astronomical Satellite.

How Phaethon makes dust is unsettled. NASA's STEREO spacecraft saw it brighten near the Sun in 2009, and Jewitt and Li (2010) proposed that the heat cracks and breaks down its rock. Zhang et al. (2023) found that the brightenings seen near perihelion since 1997 are glowing sodium, not dust, so how the dust of the Geminid stream was shed remains an open question.

panels.title: The best shower of the year
body: In early December, Earth starts running into Phaethon's dust. The Geminids are one of the richest and most reliable meteor showers of the year.
On a clear, dark night at their best you might see about two meteors a minute. They get going in mid-evening, too, so you don't have to stay up until dawn.
details: Active 4 to 17 December 2019, peak on 14 December between 02:00 and 23:00 UT, so the peak night is 13 to 14 December (International Meteor Organization); zenithal hourly rate 150 (American Meteor Society; the International Meteor Organization lists 140 for 2019). NASA gives up to 120 an hour under perfect conditions and 40 to 50 an hour under typical dark skies; "about two a minute" is NASA's 120 an hour.
NASA: the shower "starts around 9 or 10 p.m."

This moment, 6 December 2019 at 00:00 UTC, is two days into the activity, chosen so that the panel opens once the shower has begun, also in the shower-only (activity) view. The rate drawn in the scene is modelled from the published peak rate.

The dots are Geminid orbits measured by the Global Meteor Network's cameras in December 2024 and December 2025. They are drawn as they are in this earlier year, 2019 to 2020: the orbits are measured, but where each dot sits along its orbit is illustrative.

panels.title: Earth reaches the thickest dust
body: Tonight Earth passes through the busiest part of the stream. Tiny specks of rock hit our air at about 35 km a second and burn up as bright streaks.
They all seem to fly out of Gemini, the Twins, which gives the shower its name.
details: The peak in this scene is 14 December 2019 at 04:33:33 UTC: the moment the Sun reaches solar longitude 261.6° (J2000), the IAU Meteor Data Center's peak, found on the engine's ephemeris. It falls inside the International Meteor Organization's 2019 peak period, 14 December between 02:00 and 23:00 UT (its single best estimate, solar longitude 262.2°, is later that day).
Radiant: right ascension 113.0°, declination +32.4° (J2000), in Gemini (IAU Meteor Data Center).
Speed: 35 km a second (22 miles a second), and the meteors tend to look yellow (NASA).
